_how: One entry per video; tools/build_case_studies.py turns these into the pages under /case-studies/. Fields: id (YouTube id), slug (page address), cat (business, economy, geopolitics or politics), h1 (page headline), seo (search-result title, under ~60 characters), desc (search-result description, under ~155 characters), lede, body (paragraphs), chapters (t = time in the video, label), countries (2-letter codes), optional series. title, published and duration come from YouTube.

case_studies.h1: Jio vs Starlink: The Billionaire Battle for India's Internet
case_studies.seo: Jio vs Starlink Explained: Who Wins India's Internet?
case_studies.desc: Musk vs Ambani, explained: how 13 telecom companies became 4, how Jio and Starlink reach you, what each costs, and both sides of the fight.
case_studies.lede: Elon Musk called Mukesh Ambani “the real boss of India.” Behind the post is a fight over who connects the next billion Indians, and what it costs you.
body: India had 13 telecom companies in 2014. After Jio launched in 2016 with free calls and data, that number fell to four, and two of them now control most broadband connections. This breakdown starts there, because the company that makes your life cheaper today can become the one you depend on tomorrow.

It then follows how your data actually travels: undersea cables, fibre and towers for Jio, a rooftop dish and satellites 550 km up for Starlink. It compares speed and price, explains why Starlink still can't sell a single connection in India, and lays out both sides of the security argument, without taking a side.

chapters.label: The billionaire battle for India's internet
How 13 telecom giants became just four
Jio vs Starlink: how your data travels
The future of India's digital landscape

case_studies.title: Jio vs Starlink: The Billionaire Battle for India's Internet

case_studies.h1: Microsoft Lost 10 Years and $7.6 Billion. So Why Is It Winning Now?
case_studies.seo: Microsoft's Comeback: From the Nokia Loss to $3 Trillion
case_studies.desc: How Microsoft wrote off $7.6 billion on Nokia, bet on boring cloud infrastructure and rebuilt its culture under Satya Nadella. Comeback, Episode 3.
case_studies.lede: Microsoft missed the smartphone, wrote off $7.6 billion on Nokia and went a decade with a flat stock price. Then it became one of the most valuable companies on Earth.
body: The final episode of The Comeback shows that the turnaround didn't start with a product. It started with Satya Nadella admitting, in public, that the Nokia deal was a mistake, and taking the loss instead of defending it.

From there it covers the unglamorous bet nobody was excited about, cloud computing through Azure, which now quietly runs the AI models people use every day, and the change in culture that turned teams competing with each other into one company competing with Google and Apple.
case_studies.title: Microsoft Lost 10 Years and $7.6 Billion. So Why Is It Winning Now?

case_studies.h1: The Rise of Walmart: 12 Years as the Biggest Company on Earth
case_studies.seo: How Walmart Became the World's Biggest Company
case_studies.desc: Sam Walton's strategy explained: small towns the giants ignored, cost discipline in the back end, and never stopping after winning. Comeback, Episode 2.
case_studies.lede: His own company said no. Kmart, Sears and Woolworths didn't even notice him. Sam Walton's small-town store went on to spend twelve straight years as the world's largest company by revenue.
body: In the 1960s every discount chain built near crowded cities. Walton built in small towns, some with fewer than 5,000 people, where nobody else bothered to compete. By the time the giants noticed Walmart, it had already won.

The episode explains how a central warehouse, its own trucks and no middlemen let Walmart cut costs in the back end and pass the savings on as “everyday low prices,” and why it kept expanding long after it had already won.

chapters.label: Going where competitors refuse to tread
Cost discipline as a competitive weapon

case_studies.title: The Rise of Walmart: 12 Years as the Biggest Company on Earth

case_studies.h1: How a Rejected Idea Became a $2 Trillion Empire
case_studies.seo: How Google Went From Rejected Idea to $2 Trillion
case_studies.desc: Yahoo and AltaVista passed on it. How Google built a better product, turned free search into AdWords, and bought Android and YouTube. Comeback, Episode 1.
case_studies.lede: Two students tried to sell their search engine for $1 million, then $750,000. Yahoo and AltaVista both said no. That idea became Google.
body: The first episode of The Comeback looks at why Google won: in 1998 search results were junk, and Larry Page and Sergey Brin simply ranked pages better, so Google improved as the internet grew while rivals got worse.

It then explains how a free product became one of the most profitable machines on the internet through AdWords, where even a small shop pays only when someone clicks, and why buying Android and a loss-making YouTube showed a company refusing to stay what it started as.

chapters.label: Why being genuinely better changed everything
Turning free services into a profit machine
Refusing to stay within the original vision

case_studies.title: How a Rejected Idea Became a $2 Trillion Empire | The Comeback Series

case_studies.h1: Your Job Is at Risk Now: AI, Layoffs and Young Workers
case_studies.seo: Is AI Taking Your Job? The Real Story Behind 2026 Layoffs
case_studies.desc: Why 22–25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs are being hit first, why AI often makes people slower, and the one skill that turns the crisis into an opportunity.
case_studies.lede: For fifteen years, learning to code was the safest career advice on the planet. Now companies that aren't even losing money are cutting staff, and young workers are hit first.
body: This breakdown looks at who is actually being cut, with real numbers: Stanford research on employment for 22-to-25-year-olds in AI-exposed jobs, tech layoffs running at around 981 a day, and a first decline in IT employment in two decades.

It also asks whether AI is really the reason, including evidence that people using AI tools can be slower while feeling faster, and why the World Economic Forum still expects millions of new jobs. The question isn't whether work disappears, but how its shape changes.

chapters.label: The end of the coding career myth
The hidden trap of AI efficiency

case_studies.title: Your JOB is in Risk Now!

case_studies.h1: Why BRICS Is Suddenly the World's Biggest Threat to the Dollar
case_studies.seo: BRICS vs the US Dollar, Explained Simply
case_studies.desc: How the dollar controls trade, what BRICS has built to get around it (the New Development Bank and local-currency payments), and whose side India is on.
case_studies.lede: Leaders from across BRICS landed in New Delhi for one summit. This isn't a foreign-policy story: it's about why your petrol, fees and the rupee depend on who controls the world's money.
body: The video explains why the dollar is powerful because of its “plumbing”: even when India buys oil from Russia, the payment usually flows through the American banking system, which can be switched off, as the world saw in 2022.

It then shows what BRICS has quietly built instead of a fantasy currency: the New Development Bank, which lends to members in their own currencies, and trade settled in rupees. And it asks the real question: with friends on every side, which side is India actually on?

chapters.label: Why global leaders are gathering in India
Three lessons from the BRICS summit

case_studies.title: Why BRICS is Suddenly the World’s Biggest Threat to Dollar?

case_studies.h1: The Death of Jaguar: How a $2.3B Icon Failed
case_studies.seo: Why Jaguar Is Failing: Six Cars Sold, Explained
case_studies.desc: Tata bought Jaguar for $2.3B in 2008 and turned it around. Then came a rebrand with no cars to sell and a cyberattack. What went wrong, and how it could recover.
case_studies.lede: In January 2026 Jaguar registered just six new cars in the UK. A year earlier it was 783. This is how India's proudest turnaround nearly came undone.
body: Tata Motors bought Jaguar Land Rover from Ford for $2.3 billion in 2008, when everyone called it reckless, and turned it into the group's biggest profit engine. The breakdown covers how big Jaguar still was, then the “Copy Nothing” rebrand launched with no cars on sale, and the 2025 cyberattack that stopped production for five weeks.
It then lays out three strategies Jaguar could use to recover, from leaving the BMW and Mercedes fight to treating operational resilience as part of the product.
case_studies.title: The Death Of Jaguar: How A $2.3B Icon Failed

case_studies.h1: ASML: The Most Important Company You Don't Know
case_studies.seo: ASML Explained: The Company Behind Every Advanced Chip
case_studies.desc: One Dutch company makes the only machines that print the world's most advanced chips. How ASML beat Nikon and Canon, and why it's at the centre of the US–China tech war.
case_studies.lede: There is one machine on Earth that can make the most advanced computer chips, and only one company builds it. Not American, not Chinese: a Dutch firm that nearly went bankrupt in 1992.
body: The breakdown explains what ASML does and how EUV lithography works in plain language, then tells the underdog story of how it overtook Japan's Nikon and Canon to hold a monopoly on the technology.

It ends at the US–China chokepoint: why Washington wants ASML locked down, why Beijing wants it opened up, how the Netherlands ended up holding a switch over China's chip industry, and what all of it means for India's own chip ambitions.

chapters.label: The underdog story: ASML vs Nikon & Canon

case_studies.title: The Most Important Company, That You Don't Know: ASML

case_studies.h1: US Debt Bomb: How It Reaches Your Money in India
case_studies.seo: The US Debt Crisis Explained, and What It Means for India
case_studies.desc: America's debt crossed $40 trillion. Why it now pays more in interest than on its military, who holds the debt, and how it reaches your rupee, petrol and EMI.
case_studies.lede: The richest country in history crossed $40 trillion in debt. The video explains how it got there, and why the blast reaches homes in India.
body: It starts with history: the same pattern of debt weakened Rome, Spain and Britain. Then it explains why this time is different, with the US now spending more on interest than on its entire military and borrowing just to keep up with payments.

The breakdown also covers who really holds the fuse, including China quietly cutting its holdings of US debt, and the two invisible wires connecting America's debt to your rupee, your petrol price and your EMI.
case_studies.title: US Debt Bomb: How To Protect Your Future ?

case_studies.h1: From Poor to the World's 4th Biggest Economy: This Is India
case_studies.seo: How India Became the World's 4th Largest Economy
case_studies.desc: In 1947 the world gave India five years to survive. The 1991 crisis, the gold pledge, a young workforce and the road to a $30 trillion economy by 2047.
case_studies.lede: In 1947 much of the world doubted India would survive. This Independence Day special traces how it became the fourth-biggest economy on Earth.

It closes on the road ahead: the goal of a $30 trillion developed nation by 2047, the power of one of the youngest workforces in the world, and the debate over whether that target is realistic.

The midnight birth of a nation

case_studies.h1: Why the Supreme Court Ordered Jet Airways to Be Liquidated
case_studies.seo: Why Jet Airways Collapsed: The 3 Decisions Explained
case_studies.desc: Jet Airways was India's proudest airline. How expansion on borrowed money, flying after the cash ran out and a rescue that never funded it led to liquidation.
case_studies.lede: Jet Airways wasn't a budget airline that cut corners. It was India's second-biggest carrier, famous for warm service and on-time flights, and in 2024 the Supreme Court ordered it liquidated.
body: Founded in 1993 by former travel agent Naresh Goyal, Jet grew to more than 100 aircraft, flying from Delhi and Mumbai to London and beyond. It didn't die from bad luck; the breakdown traces three decisions.

Expanding on borrowed money at the wrong time, including the costly Air Sahara deal. Flying long after the money had run out. And a rescue plan whose winning bidders never put in the funds. The finale of the DTKT series ties all three companies together.

chapters.label: How great Jet Airways actually was

case_studies.title: Why Supreme Court Ordered The Greatest Airline to liquidate??  | DTKT Series 3/3

case_studies.h1: Evergrande: How the World's Biggest Property Developer Collapsed
case_studies.seo: Why Evergrande Collapsed: China's Property Giant Explained
case_studies.desc: Evergrande built homes in hundreds of Chinese cities, then collapsed. Selling homes before building them, borrowing at an impossible scale, and inflating revenue.
case_studies.lede: Evergrande wasn't a fraud pretending to be a company. It was a real empire, which is what makes its collapse so frightening: around 1.5 million families paid for homes that were never finished.
body: Hui Ka Yan started with almost nothing and built China's largest property developer, building in more than 200 cities and owning a football club, a water brand and an electric-car company. Today the company has been wound up by a Hong Kong court and removed from the stock exchange.

The breakdown traces three decisions: selling homes before building them to fund the next project, borrowing on a scale no company should, and inflating revenue instead of facing the truth, as regulators later found.
case_studies.title: The Reason Why World's Greatest Infrastructre Brand Collapsed | DTKT Series 2/3

case_studies.seo: Why BYJU'S Collapsed: The $22 Billion Story Explained
case_studies.desc: A teacher from Kerala built a $22 billion edtech giant with 100 million students. Four years later it was worth almost nothing. The three decisions behind it.
case_studies.lede: BYJU'S was not a scam, which is what makes it painful. A teacher who filled stadiums built the world's most valuable edtech company, sponsored India's cricket jersey and the FIFA World Cup, and then lost it all.
body: The first episode of the DTKT series shows how big BYJU'S really was at its peak: a $22 billion valuation and 100 million students.

It then breaks down the three decisions that brought it down, and the lesson hidden inside each one. Where matters are still disputed in court, the video treats them as allegations or as the findings of a specific court.
case_studies.title: BYJU'S $22 Billion Gamble: Played with Kids Future ? | DTKT Series 1/3

case_studies.title: From Textile Shop to Jewellery Empire | The Kalyan Jewellers Strategies to be world No.1

body: India was invited to the G7 for the 13th year in a row, and is still not a member. The video looks at what was decided over three days in Evian, including the US statement that it would defend India.

It explains which country walked out stronger, which walked out exposed, and the one sentence from an Indian leader that almost no camera caught, which the video argues was the most important of the summit.
case_studies.title: US Will Defend India — On One Condition to MODI that Nobody Noticed...

case_studies.h1: A Country With No Water Became Richer Than Britain
case_studies.seo: How Singapore Got Rich With No Resources
case_studies.desc: No oil, no farmland, not even its own water. How Lee Kuan Yew built Singapore into one of the richest nations, and the biggest foreign investor in India.
case_studies.lede: Singapore had no oil, no farmland and couldn't even make its own drinking water. Today it is richer per person than Britain, and the single biggest foreign investor in India.
body: Thrown out of Malaysia in 1965, Singapore started with 2 million people, no resources and riots in the streets. The video explains Lee Kuan Yew's bets: war on corruption, English as the working language, and home ownership for most of the population.

It then shows how a port on the Strait of Malacca became a tollbooth on world trade, how Temasek and GIC invest the country's money like an investor rather than a government, and the lessons India keeps refusing to learn.
case_studies.title: A Country With No Water Became Richer Than Britain — And India Keeps Ignoring

case_studies.h1: Nvidia: The Brain Behind Every AI
case_studies.seo: How Nvidia Went From 30 Days to Bankruptcy to AI Giant
case_studies.desc: Nvidia's first chip failed, 249,000 of 250,000 units came back, and it was 30 days from shutting down. How CUDA and AI made it worth trillions.
case_studies.lede: The company powering the AI revolution was once 30 days from shutting down. Its first product failed so badly that customers returned 249,000 out of 250,000 units.
body: The video follows Jensen Huang from a bet on 3D graphics for video games, through the NV1 failure and the risky RIVA 128 chip that saved the company, to CUDA, a platform that had almost no users for six years.

Then AlexNet ran on Nvidia chips in 2012, and AI took off. The breakdown also covers why most AI now runs on Nvidia hardware, how the company became a geopolitical weapon, and includes a three-question game along the way.

chapters.label: The game: can you score 3 out of 3?
The failure that nearly killed Nvidia
Nvidia and the birth of AI

case_studies.title: The Brain Behind Every AI — Every AI depends on this.. | Untold Strategy Revealed

case_studies.seo: West Bengal's Economic Decline, Explained in 3 Decisions
case_studies.desc: In 1951 West Bengal had more factories than Maharashtra and Gujarat combined. Three decisions across three governments, and the business lessons in each.
case_studies.lede: In 1951 West Bengal ran 27% of India's industrial output, and Kolkata was richer than Mumbai. Today the state ranks 24th in per-capita income. The video asks how.
body: Timed with the 2026 election result, the breakdown looks past the celebrations to a longer question: why Bengal's economy declined. It traces three decisions across three governments over seventy years.

case_studies.h1: India's GDP Rank Fell. But Is This Planned?
case_studies.seo: Why India's GDP Rank Fell to 6th Despite 8% Growth
case_studies.desc: India grew at 8.2% and still fell from 4th to 6th. The calculation behind it, how US interest rates hit the rupee, India's real rank, and how to protect your money.
case_studies.lede: India became the world's fourth-largest economy in 2023, then dropped to sixth in 2026. No war, no scam, no recession: it grew 8.2% and still fell two places.
body: The video explains the one calculation behind the drop: GDP rankings are measured in US dollars, so a weaker rupee shrinks India's number even while its economy grows. It shows how American interest rates pushed the rupee down, and why a shrinking Germany can still rank above a growing India.
It then looks at India's rank by purchasing power, which tells a very different story, and ends with three practical things viewers can do to protect their own money.

chapters.label: India's real rank nobody talks about

case_studies.title: India’s GDP Rank Fall… But Is This Planned??

case_studies.lede: During the 1971 war, when major powers lined up against India, one country stood with it: the Soviet Union. That moment still shapes India's choices today.

case_studies.desc: In 1997 Apple was burning $1M a day with 90 days left. Steve Jobs' three moves, the iPod and iPhone, and how Tim Cook took Apple from $350B to $3.77T.

case_studies.h1: Why the World Is Betting Big on India's AI
case_studies.seo: India AI Impact Summit 2026: Why the World Is Investing
case_studies.desc: In 1991 India airlifted its gold to stay solvent. In 2026 the world pledged ₹1.6 lakh crore at the India AI Impact Summit. What changed, in 3 lessons.
case_studies.lede: In 1991 India secretly flew 67 tonnes of gold abroad because it had no money left. In 2026 the world brought around ₹1,60,000 crore into India in six days.
body: The video breaks down the India AI Impact Summit 2026: who invested, what was announced, and why the world is now betting on India.

To explain how the country got here, it goes back to the 1991 crisis and the gold pledge, the reforms that followed, the IT boom and UPI, and turns the story into three simple lessons for students and citizens.
case_studies.title: Why the World Is Betting Big on India’s AI (AI Summit 2026 | Power, Money & Strategy)

case_studies.h1: Iran Just Shut Down the World Without Firing a Shot
case_studies.seo: Strait of Hormuz Crisis 2026 Explained: Why Oil Matters
case_studies.desc: A 33 km strip of water between Iran and Oman stopped 150 oil tankers. What the Strait of Hormuz is, why most of its oil goes to Asia, and what it means for India.
case_studies.lede: In late February 2026, tankers stopped moving through a 33-kilometre strip of water between Iran and Oman, and the global economy felt it within days.
body: The video explains what the Strait of Hormuz is, why there is no real alternative route, and why most of the oil that passes through it goes to Asia, not the West, which makes it India's problem as much as anyone's.
It follows the 2026 crisis timeline, the jump in oil prices and the losses for major brands, the reopening, what India did, and the lessons for India and for viewers.

case_studies.h1: From IIT Dorm to Market Leader: Ather's Exact Formula
case_studies.seo: Ather Energy's Growth Story, Explained
case_studies.desc: From an IIT hostel in 2013 to a ₹26,756 crore market cap in 2025: how Ather Energy grew while other electric-scooter brands struggled.
case_studies.lede: Ather started in an IIT hostel in 2013. By 2025 it was a listed company worth ₹26,756 crore, growing while other electric-scooter brands struggled.
body: This long-form breakdown follows Ather Energy's journey, the real data behind its growth, and how it positioned itself in India's electric two-wheeler market.
It closes with three hard truths from the story for students, founders and professionals.
